title: Recommissioning a stored Panhard Dyna Z12: checks in controlled stages
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: Recommissioning separates engine, fuel, cooling, electrics, brakes and running gear. Each stage needs confirmation before the next begins.
content:
The first start of a long-stored Dyna Z12 brings instant satisfaction. It can also send tank debris into the carburettor, turn an engine without prior checks or suggest that a car capable of moving is ready for the road. Durable recommissioning has a different purpose: establish a baseline and make progress without adding failures to those already present.

Define the starting point

Storage duration, conditions and the reason the car stopped shape the programme. A running car put away two years ago differs from one abandoned in 1985 after an unknown fault. Record invoices, service labels, old notes, displayed mileage and removed parts before altering settings.

Photograph engine compartment, underside, dashboard and connections. An unusual wire may be an error or an adaptation whose purpose will disappear if dismantled too quickly. Create three lists: safety, functions required for starting and work required before movement.

The shell comes before the engine

A weakened structure cannot be lifted or moved like a sound car. Floors, sills, crossmembers and suspension mountings are assessed before winching or placing it on stands. All four wheels need to turn without tearing a seized line or forcing a suspension component.

Storage also attracts damp, rodents and insects. Remove nests, displaced insulation and blocked ducts with suitable protection. On an air-cooled engine, debris around the turbine or under shrouding can obstruct cooling as well as create dirt.

Identify the engine and confirm free movement

Z12 used M5 and, for the 1958 model year, M5 Aérodyne with turbine and panels directing cooling air. Photograph plates, carburettor, ignition and air system before ordering parts. An exchange engine requires information for the unit actually installed.

Mechanical rotation is checked without asking the starter to overcome a tight point. Oil condition, leaks, fasteners and complete shrouding add to the interpretation. If rotation is uneven, internal noise appears or cooling parts are absent, diagnosis stops before starting.

Restore the fuel path from the tank

Old fuel degrades, leaves deposits and attacks some hoses. Tank, lines, pump and carburettor form one circuit: cleaning only the float chamber leaves the source of contamination untouched. Hard, cracked or unknown hoses are replaced with material compatible with current fuel.

An auxiliary supply carries a fire risk and must not become an improvised permanent arrangement. Ventilation, an appropriate extinguisher, no leaks and constant supervision are essential. Use a professional where wiring, carburettor condition or safe fuel pressure is uncertain.

Electrics under control

Before connecting a battery, confirm voltage and polarity against the existing installation. Inspect cables, terminals, earths, insulation and passages beside metal. A bare wire or poor earth may heat while the starter performs badly. Added accessories, especially without identified protection, are documented and isolated if necessary.

Initial electrical tests proceed by function: general supply, lamps and signals, then starter after mechanical preparation. This sequence localises faults and avoids loading the entire harness during investigation.

The first start remains a short test

Once lubrication, fuel, ignition, cooling and electrics have been checked, start in a ventilated space with one person driving and another watching for leaks. Pressure, sound, smoke, stability and temperature change matter from the first seconds. Repeated throttle blips prove nothing useful.

After stopping, inspect connections, underside and fluid levels again. Compare cold behaviour with the restart. A satisfactory result permits a longer stationary test; metallic noise, a fuel leak or abnormal heat returns the process to diagnosis.

Brakes are an independent project

A firm pedal does not establish the state of master cylinder, wheel cylinders, hoses, pipes or drums. After long storage, the complete hydraulic circuit deserves inspection. An internal leak may leave no puddle, while a hose can look sound outside and fail internally.

Drums are removed by the appropriate method, linings and mechanisms checked, then the circuit restored and bled with the fluid specified in documentation. Until balance and absence of leakage are confirmed, the engine may run but the car does not enter public roads.

Tyres, bearings, steering and suspension

Tread depth is insufficient evidence for old tyres. Date, cracking, storage deformation and valves determine replacement. Rims, fasteners, bearings and play are checked while each wheel is accessible.

Steering should cover its travel without a tight point. Joints, pivots, springs, torsion bars, dampers and mountings are inspected according to Dyna Z design. Old grease or fresh paint does not replace a play check. Ride height and stance after a few movements also provide evidence.

Transmission and controls before movement

The four-speed gearbox, clutch and controls may seize in storage. With engine stopped, check movement without force. Lubricant level and condition, boots, linkages and leaks are recorded. An immobile pedal or lever needs local investigation rather than more pressure.

Driveshafts and their protection belong in the front-end check. The first movement may expose a stuck clutch, noisy transmission or vague control, but takes place in a clear private area at very low speed.

Three gates before road use

  1. Stationary: stable engine, no dangerous leak, charging and cooling monitored.
  2. Controlled movement: a few metres, even braking, free steering, usable clutch and gearbox.
  3. Progressive distance: short loop with an easy stopping point, complete inspection, then gradual increase.

Each gate produces a written list. Outside temperature, duration, noises, levels before and after, brake behaviour and checked fasteners show whether the situation improves. One successful journey does not end recommissioning; it produces new observations under load.

Preserve what the process reveals

Part references, settings found and photographs before cleaning join the vehicle file. They support future maintenance and stop a later modification being mistaken for factory assembly. Careful recommissioning makes the Dyna usable while preserving its mechanical history.
